preamble: In Northern Berber languages the voiced uvular fricative [ʁ] (written ⟨ɣ⟩) has no geminate of its own: whenever it is geminated, typically in the imperfective (intensive) stem of verbs, it surfaces as the voiceless uvular stop [qː]. Gemination thus brings fortition and devoicing together, alongside the parallel alternations w ~ bb/ggʷ and y ~ gg. The pattern is synchronic and morphophonemic. Proto-Berber reconstructions already pair singleton *ɣ with geminate *qq, so it is not a recent diachronic change. It is described for Kabyle, Tashelhit (Shilha), Tarifit and the Ayt Ndhir variety of Central Atlas Tamazight.

examples.to: qqar [qːar] (imperfective), as in qqareɣ taktabt 'I am reading a book'
examples.note: Gemination turns fricatives and semivowels into stops: geminated ɣ becomes qq, geminated y becomes gg and geminated w becomes bb.

examples.to: aqqra [aqːra] (imperfective), as in ar yaqqra 'he is reading'
examples.note: Under morphological gemination ɣɣ is realized as qq and labialized ɣɣ° as qq°.
Same imperfective gemination; the derived agent noun amqqrs 'slaughterer' also has qq.

examples.to: qqar [qːar] (imperfective): qqareɣ 'I read', yeqqar 'he reads', qqaren 'they read'
examples.note: The imperfective stem replaces the singleton fricative with the geminate uvular stop throughout the paradigm.
In Ayt Ndhir the geminate correspondents of /ʁ, dˤ, ʃ, ʒ, w, j/ are usually /qː, tˤː, t͡ʃː, d͡ʒː, ɣʷː, ɣː/; some native words keep /ʁː/ instead.
